name: Interpretability Methods Benchmark
description: We propose an empirical measure of the approximate accuracy of feature importance estimates in deep neural networks. Our results across several large-scale image classification datasets show that many popular interpretability methods produce estimates of feature importance that are not better than a random designation of feature importance. Only certain ensemble based approaches---VarGrad and SmoothGrad-Squared---outperform such a random assignment of importance. The manner of ensembling remains critical, we show that some approaches do no better then the underlying method but carry a far higher computational burden.
evaluation_method: rank-correlation (e.g., Spearman) and randomization/sanity tests comparing importance maps to randomized baselines
general_score_metric: Spearman rank correlation (or other rank/correlation metrics) against ground-truth or randomized baselines
typical_sota_score: Many methods score near-random (≈0–0.2 correlation); certain ensemble methods (e.g., VarGrad/SmoothGrad-Squared) can achieve higher (~0.2–0.5) depending on settings
reputation: Highly influential—widely cited for highlighting serious limitations in popular saliency/interpretability methods and prompting follow-up work.
notes: Non-LLM, vision-focused benchmark; results depend heavily on the choice of model/dataset and ensembling strategy; some evaluation variants are computationally expensive; the benchmark exposes that many methods do not outperform random baselines.
